summary:
GeoAnalog Matchmaker is a browser-based scientific tool that matches Earth locations to planetary analog environments on Mars, Europa, Titan, the Moon, and seven other bodies. It runs fully offline as a single self-contained HTML file (~2.63 MB).

The app features an Earth Analog Atlas of 18 verified field stations — volcanic, hyperarid, polar, evaporite, and subsurface — each with real DEM-derived elevation profiles sourced from Copernicus GLO-30, USGS 3DEP, NASADEM, and ArcticDEM. A Terrain Panorama renders each station as a wide planetary landscape using actual elevation geometry — no synthetic heights. Surface colors adapt per location using 13 peer-reviewed material palettes (basalt, salt, ice, sand, sulfur, and more).

A Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis engine scores and ranks analog matches by climate, geology, and atmospheric parameters. All data sources, DEM providers, resolution, CRS, and licenses are displayed transparently. 215 tests pass across 12 suites.
details:
GeoAnalog Matchmaker is a browser-based scientific tool that identifies Earth locations that physically resemble environments on other planets. It works by comparing geophysical, geological, and climatological characteristics of 18 verified Earth analog field stations against 10 planetary target environments — including Mars, the Moon, Europa, Titan, and Enceladus — using a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis engine. The user selects a planetary target, adjusts similarity weights across criteria such as temperature range, atmospheric pressure, surface geology, and UV index, and the engine returns a ranked list of the most analogous Earth locations with a full scientific dossier.

The application features an interactive Earth Analog Atlas with three visualization modes: Esri satellite imagery for overhead site inspection, a physical topographic map for regional context, and a unique Terrain Panorama mode that renders a wide, stylized planetary landscape using real elevation geometry fetched from verified Digital Elevation Model sources. The terrain silhouette is never procedurally generated — it comes exclusively from measured elevation samples. Surface material colors adapt per location based on peer-reviewed spectral and lithological data, so a Bolivian salt flat looks distinctly different from an Antarctic dry valley or a Hawaiian lava field.

The intended impact is to support planetary scientists, educators, and mission planners in visualizing and communicating why specific Earth locations serve as research proxies for other worlds — making analog science more accessible and visually intuitive without sacrificing scientific integrity.

The project was built entirely with vanilla JavaScript and HTML Canvas, using Vite as the build tool and MapLibre GL JS for the raster map layers. No UI framework dependency was introduced. It ships as a single self-contained offline HTML file (~2.63 MB) requiring no server or internet connection after download. Elevation data is sourced from Copernicus DEM GLO-30, USGS 3DEP, NASADEM/SRTM, and ArcticDEM, selected automatically per station based on geographic coverage and latitude. Surface material definitions reference the USGS Spectral Library, ESA WorldCover, ISRIC SoilGrids, and over 18 peer-reviewed field studies. All 215 automated tests pass across 12 test suites.

Creativity comes from the intersection of serious planetary science and accessible visual storytelling. Rather than showing raw data tables, the tool transforms real elevation profiles into immersive panoramic landscapes with environment-appropriate skies, atmospheric haze, and geologically grounded surface textures — while keeping the underlying numbers fully auditable. Every rendered scene links directly to its DEM provider, dataset ID, resolution, vertical datum, and license, so the visualization is beautiful but never misleading.

Key factors the team considered included scientific honesty (missing data is always labeled as unavailable, never substituted), offline accessibility (the entire app works without a network connection), geographic correctness (each DEM provider is chosen based on actual coverage boundaries, not convenience), and visual clarity (vertical exaggeration is display-only and always shown to the user so it is never confused with true terrain geometry).
